title: Napkin Math
subtitle: Turn 'ten million daily users' into requests per second, terabytes, and gigabits in a few lines of arithmetic.
learn: Convert daily active users into average and peak requests per second
Estimate how fast storage grows and what a year of data costs in space
Convert photo or video sizes into bandwidth, and avoid the bits-versus-bytes trap
Recall the latency numbers that separate memory, SSD, network, and distance
Use powers of two and round numbers to do all of this in your head

steps.title: Will it fit on one machine?
steps.body: You are designing a photo-sharing app with 10 million daily active users (DAU, people who open it each day). Before drawing any boxes, ask: how many requests per second, how much storage, how much network traffic? Napkin math answers these in minutes with rough numbers. It tells you whether one server is enough or you need a fleet.
steps.idea: Estimate first. Being within 2x to 3x is good enough to choose a design.
steps.caption: Ten million daily users, and nothing else is known yet.

steps.title: Round numbers are your friend
steps.body: Use round numbers. A day has 86,400 seconds, which we round to 100,000 (10^5). So 1 million requests a day is about 10 per second (really 11.6). For sizes, remember that 2^10 is about a thousand (KB), 2^20 a million (MB), 2^30 a billion (GB) and 2^40 a trillion (TB). Errors of 10 to 20 percent do not matter here. We also state our assumptions: each user views 100 photos a day, and 10% of users upload one photo.
steps.idea: Memorise 86,400 seconds per day and the powers-of-two ladder. Most estimates then become counting zeros.
steps.caption: Assumptions: 100 views per user per day; 10% of users upload one photo.

steps.title: From DAU to QPS
steps.body: Reads per day: 10M users × 100 views = 1 billion. Divide by about 86,400 seconds and you get about 12,000 reads per second on average. This is called QPS (queries per second). We assume each view makes one API call for photo details, while the image bytes come from the CDN. Uploads: 10% of users post one photo, so 1M a day, about 12 writes per second. Reads outnumber writes about 1000 to 1, so this system must be built for fast reads.
steps.idea: QPS = (DAU × actions per user per day) ÷ 86,400. The read/write ratio shapes the design.
steps.caption: On average, about 12,000 reads per second hit the system.

steps.title: Design for the peak
steps.body: Traffic is not flat. People browse photos in the evening, so the busiest hour can be several times the average. A common rule of thumb is peak = 2x to 5x average. We use 3x, which gives about 36,000 reads per second. Servers must handle the peak, not the average. Otherwise the app breaks exactly when most people are watching.
steps.idea: Size capacity for the peak: multiply the average by a peak factor (a rule of thumb, often 2x to 5x).
steps.caption: At peak: about 36,000 reads per second (3 × 12,000).

steps.title: Storage grows every day
steps.body: One million uploads a day at about 2 MB each is 2 TB per day. Over 365 days that is about 730 TB, close to three quarters of a petabyte (PB, 1,000 TB). That is before making backup copies. Databases usually keep 3 full copies for safety, so about 2.2 PB. Large object stores often use erasure coding (splitting data with extra repair pieces), which costs closer to 1.5x. Resized copies and metadata add a bit more, so we ignore them in a napkin estimate.
steps.idea: Storage per year = writes per day × size per item × 365, then multiply by the number of copies.
steps.caption: Uploads pile up in object storage: 2 TB per day, 730 TB per year.

steps.title: Bandwidth: watch bits and bytes
steps.body: Each view serves a resized image of about 200 KB. A billion views a day is 200 TB a day, or about 2.3 GB per second. Network links are rated in bits, not bytes, so multiply by 8: about 18 Gbps on average and 55 Gbps at peak. That is far too much for the main servers. A CDN keeps copies of popular files on servers near users, so most of these bytes never touch the origin. Egress means data leaving your system.
steps.idea: Bandwidth = QPS × bytes per response. Multiply bytes by 8 to compare with link speeds in bits.
steps.caption: About 18 Gbps leaves the system, mostly served from CDN caches.

steps.title: Latency numbers to remember
steps.body: Some speeds are worth remembering. Reading memory takes about 100 nanoseconds. An SSD random read takes about 100 microseconds. A round trip inside one data center takes about 0.5 ms. A spinning-disk seek takes about 10 ms. A round trip between continents takes about 150 ms. Each step down this ladder is roughly 5 to 1000 times slower, so keep slow tiers off the hot path. The animation shows why: the cache answers fast and the disk-based database answers slowly.
steps.idea: Memory is about 1000x faster than SSD, and a cross-continent round trip is about 300x slower than one inside a data center.
steps.caption: A cache lookup is much cheaper than a database read from disk.

steps.title: Turning numbers into decisions
steps.body: Now divide the estimate by what one machine can do. Say one API server handles 2,000 requests per second. Peak 36,000 needs 18 servers, so plan about 25 for headroom. One database comfortably serves about 5,000 simple reads per second. A cache hit means the answer was already in the cache. A miss falls through to the database. At most 5,000 of 36,000 lookups (about 14%) can reach the database, so the cache must hit about 86% of the time. At 85% you would send 5,400 misses, too many, so aim for 90%. Then the database sees 3,600 per second, under its 5,000 limit.
steps.idea: Divide the estimate by what one machine can do. The result tells you how many machines, or what cache hit rate, you need.
steps.caption: The cache absorbs most reads, so the database sees only misses.

steps.title: What if they were videos?
steps.body: Change one assumption: each upload is a 50 MB video instead of a 2 MB photo. Storage becomes 1M × 50 MB = 50 TB per day, which is about 18,000 TB (18 PB) per year. That is 25 times more. Nothing else in the estimate changed, yet the cost and design of the storage layer changed completely. One input can dominate everything, so check the biggest ones first.
steps.idea: Find the assumption that moves the result most and sanity-check that one first.
steps.caption: Same upload rate, 25x the bytes written.

steps.title: The napkin recipe
steps.body: State your assumptions, then convert. Users to QPS: divide by 86,400. Average to peak: multiply by about 3. Items to storage: size × count × days. Responses to bandwidth: bytes × 8 for bits. Then compare each result with what one machine can do and with the latency ladder. Answers within a factor of 2 to 3 are enough to choose a design.
steps.idea: Write assumptions down, round aggressively, and use the results to choose between one box and a fleet.
steps.caption: Our photo app: 12k QPS, 36k peak, 730 TB a year, 18 Gbps.

quiz.q: An app has 5 million DAU, and each user makes 20 requests a day. What is the average QPS, roughly?
quiz.why: 5M x 20 = 100M requests per day. Dividing by about 100,000 seconds per day gives about 1,000, or 1,160 with 86,400. Peak would be several times that.

quiz.q: 300,000 uploads a day at 5 MB each, kept for one year with no replication. About how much storage is that?
quiz.why: 300,000 x 5 MB = 1.5 TB per day. Times 365 is about 550 TB. Replication would multiply that further.

quiz.q: You serve 1.2 GB per second on average and your network link is 10 Gbps. What does the napkin math say?
options: It barely fits on average and cannot absorb peak
It fits easily, since 1.2 is far smaller than 10
It fits, since 10 Gbps is 10 GB/s
It is fine as long as peak is under 2x
quiz.why: Link speeds are in bits: 1.2 GB/s x 8 = 9.6 Gbps, already about 96 percent of the link. Any peak above average would saturate it.

quiz.q: Peak reads are 30,000 per second and your database safely handles 5,000. About what cache hit rate do you need at minimum?
quiz.why: The database may see at most 5,000 of 30,000 requests, which is about 17 percent misses, so a hit rate of roughly 83 percent. 85 percent meets it; 70 percent leaves 9,000 misses, and 50 percent leaves 15,000.

cheatsheet.def: 86,400, rounded to about 100,000 (10^5). So 1 million events per day is about 12 per second.
2^10 is about 1 thousand (KB), 2^20 about 1 million (MB), 2^30 about 1 billion (GB), 2^40 about 1 trillion (TB), 2^50 about 1 quadrillion (PB).
QPS = queries (requests) per second. Average QPS = DAU x actions per user per day / 86,400. Peak QPS = average x 2 to 5 (rule of thumb; 3 is a common default).
Per year = items per day x bytes per item x 365. Multiply by the replication factor, usually 3 for databases, about 1.5 for erasure-coded object storage, for the real footprint.
QPS x bytes per response gives bytes per second. Multiply by 8 for bits per second, which is how network links are rated.
Memory about 100 ns, SSD read about 100 us, same-data-center round trip about 0.5 ms, disk seek about 10 ms, cross-continent round trip about 150 ms.
Divide peak load by what one machine handles to get a server count, then add headroom. Do the same for a database against cache miss rate.
